bullets: How to split an L-shape into two rectangles to find its area, and walk every edge to find its perimeter
slides.heading: Area and perimeter of an L-shape
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we split an L-shape into two rectangles, add their areas to get 40 800, and walk all six edges to get a perimeter of 920 - and by the end you will be able to explain why the empty corner adds no area.

bullets: Split a composite shape into rectangles: part A is 200 by 120 and part B is 120 by 140
Add the part areas: 24 000 + 16 800 = 40 800
Walk every side for the perimeter, including the inner steps of the L
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: The L-shape fits inside a box that is 200 by 260, and 200 x 260 = 52 000
But part of that box is empty - is 52 000 really the area of the L?
slides.heading: Is the area just length times width?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands: is the area 52 000, or is it smaller? Take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: hold on to your idea, because scene s3 settles this exactly.

bullets: Area counts only the filled parts: split the L into rectangles and add their areas
Perimeter is the walk around the whole edge: add all six side lengths
slides.heading: Split for area, walk for perimeter
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: split and add for area, and walk every edge - including the inner steps - for perimeter.

bullets: Part A is 200 by 120, so its area is 200 x 120 = 24 000
Part B is 120 by 140, so its area is 120 x 140 = 16 800
slides.heading: Two rectangles make one L
slides.notes: Narrate the L splitting apart into its two rectangles and coming back together: part A on top, part B below, with no overlap and nothing left over.

bullets: The six edges are 200, 120, 80, 140, 120 and 260
slides.heading: Trace the edge for the perimeter
slides.notes: Follow the arrow around the edge slowly and call out each side as it is walked: do not skip the two inner steps of the L.

bullets: The bounding box is 200 by 260 = 52 000, but its corner is empty
The real area counts only the filled parts: 24 000 + 16 800 = 40 800
slides.heading: Watch out: the missing corner has no area
slides.notes: Hold the box outline up against the L: the box counts an empty corner that was never filled, so 52 000 overcounts the area.

bullets: For a composite figure, add the areas of the parts
Walk every side for the perimeter: this L has perimeter 920 and area 40 800
slides.heading: The takeaway
slides.notes: Land the summary: split and add for the area, walk every edge for the perimeter - the two jobs use different moves.

slides.heading: Worked example: split and add the area
slides.notes: Talk through the split-and-add working slowly as in scene s1 and name each step as you write it; say: adding the two part areas, never the box, gives 40 800.

bullets: Split the L into part A and part B and find the total area, showing the working
List all six edge lengths of the L and add them to find the perimeter
slides.heading: Your turn: split, add and walk
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on the two part areas first, then on whether they counted the inner step edges.

bullets: On your own: find the area of the L by splitting it into two rectangles
Explain in one sentence why the empty corner adds no area
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the split-and-add working in your first answer, plus one clear sentence about the empty corner in your second.
